p: The poet Hesiod, a Greek farmer who lived some seven hundred years before Christ and wrote a gloomy poem called Works and Days, divided the history of mankind into ages named after metals: a golden age, when men lived like gods without toil; a silver age, more foolish; a bronze age, warlike and violent; an age of heroes; and finally his own iron age, in which men labour and suffer without rest and children dishonour their parents. It is a pleasing irony that the antiquaries of my century, quite independently and for entirely practical reasons, should have divided the past in much the same way, naming its ages after stone, bronze and iron. Hesiod thought that each age was worse than the last. The antiquaries think each was better. I suspect each was both.

The first metals used by mankind were those which can be found in nature in their pure state: gold, and copper, and occasionally iron that has fallen from the sky in meteorites. These were hammered cold into ornaments long before anyone thought of melting them. The great discovery was smelting: that certain green and blue stones, heated very hot in a fire with charcoal, would yield liquid copper. Where and how this was first learned is not certain, but the Encyclopaedia reports evidence of smelting in the Balkans and in Persia some seven thousand years ago. The heat required, more than a thousand degrees by the modern scale, was perhaps first reached in the kilns of potters, who had long been making ever hotter fires to harden their pots.

Copper alone is soft. A copper axe will cut, but it dulls quickly. The decisive improvement came when smiths found that copper melted together with a small amount of tin, about one part in ten, makes a far harder metal, which we call bronze. It is also easier to cast, flowing readily into moulds of stone or clay. With bronze one could make swords, which are impossible in stone, and axes, spear-heads, armour, cauldrons, mirrors and statues of great beauty.
## Why bronze made the world smaller

Here lies the most interesting feature of the Bronze Age, which began in the Near East about five thousand three hundred years ago and in Britain somewhat later. Copper and tin are seldom found in the same place. Tin in particular is rare. To make bronze, therefore, a people must trade, often over very great distances. Tin came to the Mediterranean from Afghanistan, from the mountains of central Europe, from Spain, and, so it is said, from Cornwall in our own island. A whole network of commerce grew up to supply it, and with the tin travelled amber from the Baltic, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, ivory from Africa, and, no doubt, ideas, fashions and diseases.

One of the most remarkable discoveries reported in the Encyclopaedia is a ship wrecked off the southern coast of Turkey, at a place called Uluburun, about three thousand three hundred years ago. It carried ten tons of copper and one ton of tin, exactly the proportion for making bronze, together with glass, ivory, ebony, gold, amber and spices, from a dozen lands. It was, in effect, a floating warehouse of the international trade of its day. That trade supported a brilliant system of kingdoms in the eastern Mediterranean: Egypt under its great Pharaohs, the Hittites of Anatolia, the Babylonians, the Mycenaean Greeks whose palace at Mycenae Herr Schliemann, having lately dug up what he declares to be Troy, now proposes, I read in the newspapers, to excavate, and the cities of Syria and Canaan. Their kings wrote letters to one another, calling one another brother, and exchanged gifts and princesses.

Then, a little after three thousand two hundred years ago, the whole system fell apart. Within a few decades, city after city around the eastern Mediterranean was burned. The Hittite empire vanished. The Mycenaean palaces were destroyed and the art of writing was forgotten in Greece for four hundred years. Egypt survived, but only after fighting off invaders whom its inscriptions call the Peoples of the Sea. The causes of this collapse are much debated, and the Encyclopaedia lists them all: drought and famine, earthquakes, rebellions, the movement of peoples, a new way of fighting on foot that defeated the chariot armies of the kings, and the breaking of the long trade routes on which bronze depended. Probably several of these came together, each making the others worse. A civilisation that depends on distant trade is rich while the trade flows and fragile when it stops. I commend this observation to the merchants of the City of London.

Iron ore, unlike tin, is found almost everywhere. Its difficulty is that it is much harder to work. It does not run liquid in an ancient furnace; it comes out as a spongy lump, called a bloom, which must be hammered while hot again and again to drive out the dross. And the iron so made is not, at first, better than bronze. Only when smiths learned to heat it in contact with charcoal, so that it took up a little carbon and became a kind of steel, and to plunge it hot into water to harden it, did iron become superior. These arts were learned slowly, perhaps first in Anatolia and the lands around it, and spread through the Near East and Europe from about three thousand two hundred years ago, and independently, the Encyclopaedia believes, in parts of Africa.

Iron changed the balance of the world. Because it was common, it was cheap. A bronze sword was the weapon of a nobleman; iron could arm a whole people, and could put an iron blade on every farmer's plough and axe, so that forests could be cleared and heavy soils tilled that had defeated earlier ages. The great empires that followed, the Assyrians, the Persians, the Romans, the Chinese of the Han, were iron empires, with armies of iron-armed infantry numbered in tens of thousands.

In a sense, we have never left the Age of Iron. My own century is built upon it: the railway, the steamship, the bridge, the factory, are iron, and lately steel, which Mr Bessemer of Sheffield has taught us to make cheaply by blowing air through molten iron. Hesiod complained that his iron age was full of toil and trouble. He did not know the half of it.
